# Studio Projects

Not every builder is on a client engagement at any given moment, and that is a matter of
arithmetic rather than merit. The Foundry runs six concurrent engagements at capacity. Each pod
seats two builders. That is twelve client seats against a cohort of thirty.

If you are not staffed, you are on a **studio project**. It is the same work held to the same
standard, without a client paying for it.

## This is not a holding pattern

A studio project is a real product with real users, built to the
[Build Standards](04-build-standards.qmd) that govern client work. It ships. It gets reviewed at
the same milestones. The only thing it lacks is an invoice.

Three reasons it matters more than it sounds.

**It is how you get staffed.** The matching rule gates eligibility on your archetype ratings, and
ratings move when you ship, not when you study. A 1 becomes a 2 the first time you build
something real in that archetype. Shipping a studio project in an archetype where you are weak is
the fastest route onto the client engagement you actually want.

**It is how the Foundry stays able to sign work.** Rule 4 of the matching rule, the two-deep rule,
requires a second builder rated 3 in the primary archetype sitting on the bench. Without that
depth we cannot sign a build phase at all. Studio projects are where the bench gets deep enough
to say yes to a client.

**It is the lab for your certification.** Client work is unpredictable and will not exercise
every skill on a schedule. A studio project is yours to shape, so you can deliberately build the
thing the [certification track](08-certification.qmd) asks for: an evaluation harness, an MCP
server, a Skill your team uses.

## Shape

| | |
|---|---|
| **Team** | Solo or a pair. No larger |
| **Hours** | The same 10 per week that a client engagement would take |
| **Duration** | One semester, extendable to two if it is going somewhere |
| **Surface** | One product surface. The same rule that governs client engagements |
| **Users** | At least three real people who are not in the Foundry, using it for their own reasons |

The user requirement is the one that makes this real. A project nobody uses is an exercise. Find
the three users before you start building, not after.

## What qualifies

A studio project has to be something a client could plausibly have paid for. In practice that
means it clears three bars:

- **It solves someone's actual problem.** Not a demo, not a tutorial reimplementation, not a
  wrapper around a model with no user in mind.
- **It uses Claude as material, not decoration.** The API, an agentic loop, an MCP integration,
  or all three. If removing the AI leaves the product intact, pick something else.
- **It runs somewhere other than your laptop.** Deployed, reachable, and running when you are
  asleep.

Faculty approves the brief in the first two weeks of the semester. Bring a one-page description
of the problem, the three users, the archetype it exercises, and what shipping looks like.

## Milestones

Studio projects run the same four milestones as client engagements, scaled to one or two
builders, and graded on the same four dimensions: correctness, usefulness, explainability, and
craft.

| Milestone | What is due |
|-----------|-------------|
| **D: Discovery** | The problem, the three users and what you learned from them, what you will build, and what you will not |
| **B1: Working build** | Software that runs, with the architecture documented |
| **B2: Shipped** | Deployed, reachable, tested, and in front of your users |
| **T: Transfer** | Documentation good enough for someone else to run it, and a decision about what happens to it next |

Transfer is not a formality. At T you decide whether the project gets handed to another builder,
opened up, folded into a Foundry engagement, or shut down honestly. Shutting something down and
saying why is a passing answer.

## How it is graded

Studio projects carry the same weight as client work. The milestone component is identical. The
one component that has no direct analog is the client's evaluation, so it is replaced.

| Component | Client engagement | Studio project |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| Milestone deliverables | Graded by faculty against the Build Standards | Identical |
| Client evaluation | Your client rates the team on five dimensions | **Your users** rate the product on the same five dimensions |
| Weekly update emails | Identical | Identical |
| Developmentship | Identical | Identical |
| Video reflection | Identical | Identical |

Your three users answer the same questionnaire the client answers: timeliness, communication,
agency, technical competency, and contribution. If you cannot get three users to answer five
questions, that is information about the project.

::: {.callout-note}
A studio project is not worth fewer points than a client engagement, and being unstaffed is not
a grade penalty. The Foundry cannot seat everyone on a client, and it would be dishonest to
build a course that quietly punishes you for that.
:::

## Getting staffed from here

Points keep accruing while you are on a studio project, capped at 300, exactly as they would
otherwise. Nothing about being on a studio project costs you standing in the auction.

If a new engagement signs and its primary archetype matches what you just shipped, say so.
Faculty calibrates archetype ratings, and a shipped studio project is the strongest evidence
available that a rating should move.

The path is short and it is the one the Foundry actually wants you to walk: ship something, raise
the rating, clear the fit gate, win the seat.
